title: What makes a system distributed
problem: Once the app runs on more than one machine, the network between them can lose, delay or duplicate messages, and no machine can tell a slow neighbour from a dead one.
summary: A distributed system is many machines that share nothing but an unreliable network. Design for partial failure: a timeout is a guess, clocks disagree, and every missing reply has at least three explanations.
catTip: I meow at the door. No answer. Are the humans out, asleep, or did my meow get lost on the way? I cannot tell. That is a distributed system, and I am its very small client.

recall.q: What is partial failure, and why does it make distributed systems hard?
recall.a: Some machines or links fail while the rest keep working. Because the only signal is silence, no node can tell a crashed peer from a slow one, so every decision about failure is a timeout-based guess that can be wrong in either direction.

guide.breaks: On one machine a call either returns or the process crashes; across a network a call can hang, succeed silently or hit a machine that is alive but unreachable, and code that assumes otherwise double-charges, deadlocks or declares healthy servers dead.
guide.tradeoffs: Every defence against an unreliable network, such as timeouts, retries, acknowledgements and replication, costs latency, duplicates or complexity, so you choose which failures to tolerate rather than eliminating them.
guide.explainSimply: A distributed system is several computers that can only talk by sending messages, and the messages behave like letters: they can be late, lost or arrive twice. Nobody has a master clock, and nobody can see whether a silent neighbour is dead or just slow. Designing for that uncertainty is what this whole track is about.
guide.hint: Think about what a missing reply tells you, then list everything it does not tell you.

meow: Meow sent. No reply. Lost meow, lost reply or slow human? A timeout is a guess, purr-haps a wrong one.

quiz.prompt: A service calls a payment API and gets no response within its timeout. Which statement is correct?
options: The payment definitely did not happen, so the service should charge again
The payment definitely happened, so the service should mark the order paid
The request may have been lost, the payment may have happened with the reply lost, or the API may be slow; the caller cannot tell which
The network must be partitioned, so the service should fail over to another region
quiz.explanation: A timeout only says that no reply arrived in time. Idempotency keys and status queries exist precisely because the caller cannot distinguish a lost request from a lost reply or a slow server.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is one of the fallacies of distributed computing?
quiz.explanation: The fallacies are the false assumptions: the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, and so on. The other three options are the true statements a design should respect.

cards.q: A remote call times out. Name three different things that could have happened.
cards.a: The request was lost; the remote processed it but the reply was lost; the remote is alive but slow (or crashed). The caller cannot tell which, so writes need idempotency keys and a way to query status.

cards.q: Which two fallacies of distributed computing does a retry storm rely on?
cards.a: "The network is reliable" (so a failure must be the server's fault and retrying is harmless) and "latency is zero" (so retrying immediately costs nothing). Backoff with jitter rejects both.

glossary.note: How machines correct their clocks against time servers; well-run servers still disagree by milliseconds.
